article.title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, January 2026 update
article.subtitle: All the numbers for every pollster, fully updated after 2025.

extraction.summary: Landing page for the January 2026 update of the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings. The update adds about 40 polls from 2025 (VA and NJ governor races, U.S. House specials) and makes no methodological changes; the method is the same as the Nate-era FiveThirtyEight ratings. The article defines every metric in the ratings: letter grade, Predictive Plus-Minus with a transparency bonus, mean-reverted bias, Simple Average Error, Simple Plus-Minus, Advanced Plus-Minus, Mean-Reverted Advanced Plus-Minus, house effects, ADPA and the herding penalty. It also gives the rules for which polls enter the database. Tables show the top pollsters' values, and downloadable files hold the raw data on more than 12,300 polls.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin pollster ratings use the same methodology as the Nate-era FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings.
findings.evidence_quote: These ratings apply the same methodology as the previous, Nate-era FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings.

findings.statement: The January 2026 update has no methodological changes from the February 2025 update. It only adds about 40 polls from 2025: the Virginia and New Jersey gubernatorial elections and the U.S. House special elections.

quantities.name: polls added
quantities.context: added for the 2025 off-year since the Feb 2025 update

findings.rationale: 2025 was an off-year, so the ratings are not expected to shift much.
findings.evidence_quote: Since there haven’t been any methodological changes since our last update

findings.statement: The pollster ratings database excludes mayoral race polls, including the 2025 New York City mayoral election, so pollsters are not penalized for misses in those races.
findings.rationale: Mayoral polling has historically not been used, and there is no principled reason to include NYC but not other mayoral races.
findings.evidence_quote: Historically, we haven’t used mayoral polling when calculating pollster ratings, and there’s no principled reason to start using polls from NYC but not from other mayoral races.

findings.statement: The pollster ratings cover all polls taken in the final 21 days before presidential, congressional and gubernatorial general elections, and before presidential primaries.

quantities.name: poll window
quantities.context: days before the election for a poll to be included in the ratings

findings.evidence_quote: In general, these ratings cover all polls in the 21 days prior to presidential, Congressional and gubernatorial general elections, and presidential primaries.

findings.statement: The pollster ratings database goes back to 1998, and polls from more recent years are weighted more heavily.
findings.evidence_quote: The database goes back to 1998, though polls from more recent years are weighted more heavily.

findings.statement: Each pollster's letter grade is based on its Predictive Plus-Minus rating.
findings.evidence_quote: An overall grade based on a pollster’s Predictive Plus-minus rating.

findings.statement: Pollsters with sparse data get rounded letter grades, such as 'A/B' instead of 'A-'.
findings.evidence_quote: Grades for pollsters with sparse data are rounded (e.g., to “A/B” rather than A-)

findings.statement: Banned pollsters automatically receive a grade of F.
findings.evidence_quote: banned pollsters automatically receive a grade of F.

findings.statement: Polls that do not meet Silver Bulletin's standards for scientific surveys are kept out of the database entirely and receive no rating. These are polls run by amateurs on cheap online survey platforms, or polls using non-random convenience samples without adequate bias correction, such as ActiVote. This is a separate category from banned pollsters.
findings.evidence_quote: These polls aren’t “banned” per se — they just don’t make it into our database in the first place because they don’t meet our standards

findings.statement: When the page was first published, five non-scientific 2025 polls had been included in the ratings database by mistake. They were later removed.
findings.evidence_quote: five polls conducted in 2025 that fall into this category were mistakenly included in our database. They have since been removed.

findings.statement: Predictive Plus-Minus is the model's projection of how much error a pollster will have in future elections relative to the average pollster. It combines the pollster's historical accuracy with its transparency and disclosure standards. Negative scores are better.
findings.evidence_quote: how accurate the model expects the pollster to be going forward based on a combination of its historical accuracy and its transparency/disclosure standards

findings.statement: Pollsters receive a transparency bonus in Predictive Plus-Minus if they are members of the AAPOR Transparency Initiative or share their data with the Roper Center archive. Either one qualifies.
findings.evidence_quote: pollsters get a bonus if they’re either a member of the AAPOR Transparency Initiative or share their data with the Roper Center archive.

findings.statement: Mean-reverted bias is a pollster's historical average statistical bias toward Democrats or Republicans, reverted toward zero by an amount that depends on its number of polls. For example, 'D+1.5' means the pollster has historically overrated Democrats by 1.5 points.

quantities.name: example bias
quantities.context: illustrative example of a pollster that overrated Democrats

findings.evidence_quote: a pollster's historical average statistical bias toward Democratic or Republican candidates, reverted to a mean of zero based on the number of polls in the database.

findings.statement: Bias is calculated only for races where exactly one Republican and one Democrat are the top two candidates, so it excludes presidential primaries.
findings.evidence_quote: This is calculated only for races in which exactly one Republican and one Democrat are the two leading candidates

findings.statement: Simple Average Error is a firm's average absolute difference between the polled margin and the actual margin separating the top two finishers.
findings.evidence_quote: calculated as the difference between the polled result and the actual result for the margin separating the top two finishers in the race.

findings.statement: Simple Plus-Minus is Simple Average Error minus the expected error for the race. Expected error accounts for the type of election, the number of days until the election, and the poll's sample size.
findings.evidence_quote: which accounts for the type of election polled, the number of days until the election, and the poll's sample size.

findings.statement: Advanced Plus-Minus also accounts for how other firms performed in the same races, and it weights recent results more heavily.
findings.evidence_quote: also accounts for the performance of other polling firms surveying the same races, and which weights recent results more heavily.

findings.statement: Mean-Reverted Advanced Plus-Minus reverts Advanced Plus-Minus toward zero. The amount of reversion depends on the firm's number of polls, with polls from earlier years discounted.
findings.evidence_quote: The amount of mean reversion is based on how many polls the firm has conducted, but with polls in previous years discounted.

findings.statement: The detailed tables list only firms with at least 20 polls, because most of the measures are not mean-reverted and carry large sampling errors. Ratings for irregular pollsters should be read with extreme caution.
findings.rationale: Non-mean-reverted measures carry large sampling error for small samples.
findings.evidence_quote: since most of these measures aren’t mean-reverted and are subject to large sampling errors.

findings.statement: House effect measures how a firm's results compare with other polls of the same race. It is distinct from statistical bias, which compares results with the actual outcome. Example: a firm shows R+3 when the other polls show a tie, so it has a Republican house effect. If the Republican wins by 5, the firm still has a 2-point Democratic bias.

quantities.name: example poll
quantities.context: hypothetical firm's result vs. a tied field

quantities.name: example bias
quantities.context: resulting bias of the hypothetical firm

findings.evidence_quote: Note that house effects are distinct from statistical bias.

findings.statement: Average Distance from Polling Average (ADPA) measures how far a firm's average poll differed from the average of other polls in the field when it was released. A low ADPA is potential evidence of herding.
findings.rationale: Herding pollsters stay suspiciously close to the consensus.
findings.evidence_quote: A low ADPA is potential evidence of herding.

findings.statement: A herding penalty applies when a firm's ADPA falls below the theoretical minimum implied by the sampling error in its polls. The penalty equals one-half of the difference between the theoretical minimum ADPA and the actual ADPA. It is added to Advanced Plus-Minus before Predictive Plus-Minus is calculated.

quantities.name: herding penalty multiplier
quantities.context: fraction of the ADPA shortfall below the theoretical minimum

findings.evidence_quote: This penalty is added to a firm's Advanced Plus-Minus score before calculating Predictive Plus-Minus.

findings.statement: The percentage of correct calls (calling the race winner) is generally a poor measure of pollster accuracy compared with polling error.
findings.evidence_quote: this is generally a poor measure of pollster accuracy compared to polling error.

findings.statement: Washington Post polls are treated as the successor to the ABC News/Washington Post partnership, so their ratings include prior ABC/Post data.
findings.rationale: ABC News discontinued its polling partnership with the Post.
findings.evidence_quote: We consider Washington Post polls to be the successor to this partnership and their ratings include prior ABC/Post data.

findings.statement:
Top Predictive Plus-Minus ratings as of Jan 12, 2026, with grade, bias and number of polls:
- Washington Post: A+, -1.09, D+0.90, 98 polls
- Marquette Law School: A/B, -1.00, D+0.32, 17 polls
- Research & Polling Inc.: A+, -0.98, R+0.55, 44 polls
- OnMessage: A, -0.85, R+1.23
- Data Orbital: A/B, -0.83
- TIPP: A, -0.81
- Cygnal: A, -0.80, D+2.04
- NYT/Siena: A, -0.80, D+1.41, 116 polls
- Monmouth: A, -0.77, D+2.00, 131 polls
- SurveyUSA: A, -0.66, 871 polls
- AtlasIntel: A, -0.64, R+0.04
- Emerson: A, -0.61, 320 polls

The tables show that grades do not map to Predictive Plus-Minus by fixed cutoffs alone. Research & Polling (-0.98) gets an A+ while Marquette (-1.00) gets A/B because of sparse data. Grades around -0.6 are A, and around -0.55 to -0.53 they are A-.

Mean reversion shrinks extreme Advanced Plus-Minus scores substantially for firms with fewer polls. Grove Insight goes from -2.51 to -0.97, and Muhlenberg from -1.85 to -0.99. SurveyUSA, with 871 polls, barely moves, from -0.83 to -0.79. Simple average errors for top firms range from 2.1 (TIPP) to 5.7 (Monmouth).

House effects can differ in sign from bias. Cygnal has an R+0.59 house effect but a D+2.04 mean-reverted bias. Other house effects include Public Opinion Strategies R+4.14, OnMessage R+3.54, Grove Insight D+3.27 and AtlasIntel R+2.00.

Herding penalties among top firms are typically +0.1 to +0.6 points. Muhlenberg College has the largest shown, about +1.2 (ADPA 3.4). ADPA values range from about 2.7 (TIPP) to 5.2 (MassINC, Susquehanna).

The released raw polls dataset contains topline numbers from more than 12,300 polls, free to use with attribution. A separate full stats file includes alternative plus-minus calculations and methodological transparency details for each pollster.
findings.evidence_quote: including topline numbers from more than 12,300 polls.
